1550:
When you call someone or something a basket case, you mean they are so overwhelmed, broken down, or dysfunctional that they can barely function at all.

It is used in two main ways:

For a person: Someone who is extremely stressed, anxious, emotionally overwhelmed, or mentally falling apart. Think of someone who is so nervous before a big exam that they can't eat, can't sleep, and can't think straight. You might say, "She was a complete basket case the night before her wedding."

For a thing, an organization, or a country: Something that is failing so badly — economically, operationally, or structurally — that it seems beyond repair. For example: "After years of mismanagement, the company became a total basket case."

The key idea in both uses is this: total inability to function properly. It's not just "struggling a little." It implies a state of near-complete breakdown.

Idioms are usually built on a visual image — a mental picture that the words originally painted. To understand "basket case," you need to understand what picture it once painted.

Imagine a person who is so utterly helpless that they cannot walk, cannot use their arms, and must literally be lifted and carried around in a basket like an object. That is the original, grim image this phrase was built on. The person is not just weak — they are completely dependent, completely unable to do anything for themselves.

Over time, this brutal physical picture was softened and extended. Instead of referring to physical helplessness, people began using it to describe emotional, mental, or functional helplessness. The basket disappeared. The idea of total breakdown stayed.
The Origin — Where Did It Come From?

This is where the history gets fascinating and a little dark.

The term appears to have originated in association with urban legends circulating in North America toward the end of the First World War (1914–18).

In its original meaning, this term comes from the US military immediately following WWI. Strangely, it was never used to describe an actual person, but only in denial of any such servicemen existing.

One of the earliest known appearances of the phrase is in an official military denial. A bulletin was issued by the U.S. Command on Public Information in March 1919, on behalf of Major General M.W. Ireland, the U.S. Surgeon General: "The Surgeon General of the Army…denies…that there is any foundation for the stories that have been circulated…of the existence of 'basket cases' in our hospitals."

So the very first time the phrase was officially documented, it was being denied. Newspapers had to explain to their readers what the term even meant. By "basket case" was meant a soldier who had lost both arms and legs and therefore could not be carried on a stretcher.

Basket cases were soldiers who had lost all of their limbs and could not be safely carried on stretchers, though these types of casualties were probably very rare. At that time, a basket case was a wicker basket used to carry linens or other dry goods.

It wasn't until World War II that the phrase prominently resurfaced. Near the end of the war in May of 1944, once again, the Surgeon General attempted to deny that there were any basket cases: "…there is nothing to rumors of so-called 'basket cases' — cases of men with both arms and legs amputated."

In short: the phrase was born from war, from the horrifying possibility of soldiers losing all four limbs, and from rumors that the military repeatedly tried to deny.
How the Meaning Shifted Over Time

The figurative sense of "a person emotionally unable to cope" is from 1921.

In the early 1950s, the phrase came to mean "a person who is emotionally or mentally unable to cope, especially because of overwhelming stress or anxiety." The dictionary's earliest example of this usage is from Polly Adler's 1953 autobiography, A House Is Not a Home: "By New Year's, 1935, after three months in the new house, I realized I'd wind up a basket case if I didn't take a vacation."

This is the turning point. The idiom moved away from its dark, literal military origins and entered everyday life as a way to describe anyone — soldier or not, physically injured or not — who was emotionally or functionally falling apart.

This term was then transferred to an emotionally or mentally unstable person, and later to anything that failed to function.
Modern Usage — All the Ways People Use It

Today, "basket case" is a very flexible idiom. Here are the main scenarios where you will hear or read it:

1. A nervous, anxious, or overwhelmed person
This is the most common use. The person doesn't have to be clinically unwell — they just have to be so stressed or panicked that they seem unable to function.

  • "I have three deadlines this week. I'm a basket case."
  • "He was a complete basket case during the job interview — shaking, sweating, forgetting his words."

2. A failing economy or country
For example: "The republics of the former Soviet Union are economic basket cases."
This use implies that the economy or country has collapsed so badly that it cannot sustain itself.

3. A failing organization or company
A company can become a basket case following poor management — for instance, GE went from America's most-valuable company to a basket case, eventually splitting in three under an outsider's management.

4. A sports team performing terribly
Even a sports team can be described as a basket case: "Chelsea looked like a basket case in the summer."
The Tone and Register — When Can You Use It?

This is important to understand as a learner.

"Basket case" is informal slang. You would use it in casual conversations, news commentary, or opinion pieces — but generally not in formal writing like academic papers or official reports.

It carries a slightly dramatic or exaggerated quality. When someone calls themselves a "basket case," they are often being self-deprecating or even a little humorous about how stressed they are. When it's used about a country or an organization, it sounds more critical and serious.

The phrase has a negative connotation — it is never a compliment. It implies failure, helplessness, or dysfunction. However, when used about oneself ("I'm a basket case right now!"), it can actually sound light-hearted or funny, like a person laughing at their own panic.

Important note: Because the original meaning referred to physically disabled soldiers, in the sense of "an amputee," this term is perceived as insulting. The modern figurative use (stressed person, failing economy) is widely accepted, but the original literal sense is considered offensive and should never be used.

You will almost always see "basket case" used with these words around it:

  • "a complete basket case" — emphasizes how total the breakdown is
  • "an absolute basket case" — same emphasis, very common
  • "turn into / become a basket case" — describes the process of falling apart
  • "end up a basket case" — the result of too much stress
  • "economic basket case" — almost a fixed phrase for a failing economy

Core meaningSomeone or something so broken down or overwhelmed that they cannot function properly
OriginWWI-era US military slang, referring (in rumor) to soldiers who had lost all four limbs
First figurative useAround 1921, then more widely from the 1950s onward
RegisterInformal / slang
Used forPeople (anxious/overwhelmed), countries (economically failing), companies/teams (dysfunctional)
ToneNegative; can be humorous when self-directed
One Sentence to Remember It By

Think of it this way: a basket case is someone or something so helpless and broken that, like a person with no limbs, they cannot carry themselves — they need to be carried.

That image — of total, complete inability to function on one's own — is the heart of this idiom, no matter how it's used today.
1551: Here is something important to know right at the start: "bass" is actually two completely different words that happen to be spelled the same way. They have different meanings, different pronunciations, and are not connected to each other at all. Each one needs to be learned separately.

This is by far the more commonly encountered meaning of "bass," and it has several related senses that all connect to one central idea: deep, low sound.

The Core Idea

Think about sound for a moment. Some sounds are high-pitched — a whistle, a child's shriek, a piccolo flute. Other sounds are low and deep — a rumbling thunder, a large drum, a growling engine. That deep, low end of sound is what "bass" refers to.

Bass is the opposite of "treble," which refers to high-pitched sounds. Together, bass and treble cover the two extremes of the range of sound.

Bass in Everyday Audio

When you use a speaker, a stereo, a car audio system, or even your phone, you will often find a "bass" control. This lets you adjust how much of the deep, low sound comes through. When people say "turn up the bass," they want more of that deep, booming quality in the audio.

A subwoofer is a special type of speaker built specifically to reproduce bass — those very low-frequency sounds you feel in your chest at a concert or in a movie theatre.

Bass in Music

In music, "bass" refers to the lowest range of musical notes and the instruments or voices that produce them.

The bass as a musical part: In almost any piece of music — whether a symphony, a pop song, or a jazz tune — there is a "bass part" or "bass line." This is the lowest layer of the music, the foundation that everything else sits on top of. It gives the music its depth, weight, and rhythmic grounding. Without the bass, music tends to feel thin and empty.

Bass instruments: Several instruments are specifically designed to play in this low register.

  • The double bass (also called the upright bass or contrabass) is the largest and lowest-pitched instrument in the string family of the orchestra. It is a tall, wooden instrument that a player stands beside and plays with a bow or by plucking the strings.
  • The bass guitar (often just called "the bass") is the low-pitched electric guitar used in rock, pop, funk, and virtually all modern music genres. It typically has four thick strings and produces that deep, rhythmic foundation you hear in any band. The bassist in a band is the person who plays it.
  • The bass drum is the large drum that sits on the floor and is hit with a padded mallet or a foot pedal. It produces a deep, powerful thud and forms the rhythmic backbone in orchestras and drum kits alike.
  • The bassoon is a large woodwind instrument in orchestras that plays in a low, dark register.
  • The bass clarinet, bass trombone, and bass saxophone are all lower-pitched versions of their respective instrument families.

The bass clef: In written music, notes are placed on a staff — a set of five horizontal lines. The bass clef is the symbol placed at the beginning of the lower staff, indicating that the notes written there are in a low range. It is one of the two most common clefs, the other being the treble clef for higher notes. Pianists, for example, read both: the right hand typically reads treble clef, and the left hand (which plays the lower notes) reads bass clef.

Bass as a Human Voice

The human voice, like instruments, comes in different ranges. When describing singing voices, "bass" refers to the lowest male singing voice. A bass singer can reach very deep, rich, resonant notes that other singers cannot.

The main categories of male singing voices, from lowest to highest, are: bass, baritone, and tenor. The bass voice is the deepest and rarest of the three. In choirs and operas, bass singers often take on roles that convey authority, gravitas, or age. Think of a deep, powerful male voice singing a church hymn or an operatic role — that is a bass voice.

There is also a bass-baritone, a voice that sits between bass and baritone — very deep, but with a little more flexibility and brightness than a pure bass.

Completely separate from the music meaning, "bass" is also the name of a type of fish. This is a real, common, edible fish found in both freshwater and saltwater environments.

The term "bass" is used for a broad group of fish, many of which are popular among anglers (people who fish for sport) and are also eaten as food.

Some well-known types include:

Largemouth bass and smallmouth bass — These are freshwater fish native to North America and are among the most popular sport fish in the world. They are named for the size of their mouths. Anglers prize them for being strong, feisty fighters when caught on a fishing line.

Striped bass — A larger fish found in both freshwater and saltwater along the North American coast. It is prized both as a sport fish and as a food fish.

Sea bass — A broader term for various ocean fish considered "bass." The European sea bass is a popular food fish in Mediterranean cooking. Chilean sea bass (actually a different species called the Patagonian toothfish, but marketed as sea bass) is widely served in upscale restaurants.

Black sea bass — A smaller saltwater fish found along the Atlantic coast of North America, commonly eaten in seafood restaurants.

In general, when someone says "I went fishing and caught a bass," they almost certainly mean one of the freshwater sport fish. When a restaurant menu lists "sea bass," it refers to one of the ocean varieties.
How to Tell Which "Bass" Is Being Used

Since these two words are spelled identically, context does all the work:

  • If someone is talking about music, sound, audio equipment, singing, or instruments — it is the music word.
  • If someone is talking about fishing, the ocean, rivers, lakes, or food/cooking — it is the fish.

There is no overlap between these two meanings. They are simply two separate words that happen to share a spelling, much like how "bank" can mean a financial institution or the side of a river.

"Bass" as a noun means either:

1. Deep, low sound — and by extension, the instruments that produce it (bass guitar, double bass, bass drum), the lowest male singing voice, the low part in music, and the low-frequency control on audio equipment.

2. A type of fish — including the largemouth bass, smallmouth bass, striped bass, sea bass, and other related species, caught for sport and eaten as food.

These two meanings have nothing to do with each other and are simply two different words that share a spelling in English.
1552: Bass-ackward (as an adverb) means doing something in completely the wrong order, in the exact opposite of the sensible or correct way, or in the most illogical, mixed-up manner imaginable. When you do something bass-ackward, you haven't just made a small mistake — you've approached it in a way that is so inside-out and upside-down that the whole thing ends up confused, inefficient, or broken before it even has a chance to work.
The "Backward" at the Heart of It

The word "backward" here doesn't just mean "in reverse" the way a video plays backward. It means your approach itself — your logic, your sequence, your method — is turned around the wrong way. You're starting from the end instead of the beginning, or working against yourself without realizing it, or doing Step 10 when you should be doing Step 1.

Think of it like trying to bake a cake by eating it first and then putting it in the oven. That's not just wrong — it's profoundly, laughably backward. That's the spirit of "bass-ackward."

"Bass-ackward" is not a mild word. It carries weight and sharpness. It signals that something has gone wrong fundamentally — not because of a small slip-up, but because the entire approach was flawed from the ground up. It often carries a tone of disbelief, frustration, or exasperated humor, like, "How did anyone think this was the right way to do it?"

This is a casual, informal American English expression. It has a folksy, colorful energy to it. It is essentially a polite stand-in for the cruder phrase "ass-backward," swapping the sounds around to soften it — so it sounds funny and harmless while still punching hard in meaning. Because of this, you'll hear it in relaxed conversation, casual writing, and everyday speech. You would not use it in a formal report, a job interview, or a professional presentation.

Here is where everything clicks. Watch how "bass-ackward" works to describe how something is done:

  • "He put the roof on the shed before building the walls — he did the whole thing bass-ackward."

(The sequence is completely reversed — he worked in the wrong order.)

  • "The government is handling this crisis bass-ackward, reacting after everything collapses instead of preventing the collapse."

(Their approach is the opposite of what logic demands.)

  • "She learned bass-ackward — memorizing the answers without ever understanding the concepts behind them."

(Her method is inverted; she skipped the foundation and started with the conclusion.)

  • "This whole plan is bass-ackward. You can't market a product that doesn't exist yet."

(The entire logic of the plan is turned around.)

In every example, notice that "bass-ackward" modifies the verb — it tells you how the action was carried out. The action was carried out in a fundamentally wrong, reversed, topsy-turvy way.
What It Implies About the Situation (or Person)

When you say something was done bass-ackward, you are implying:

  • The natural, logical order was ignored or violated.
  • The result is confusion, inefficiency, or failure — because you can't build on a faulty foundation.
  • There's often a sense that a little common sense could have prevented the whole mess.
  • It doesn't always mean the person is stupid — sometimes it means they were misguided, rushed, or working with bad assumptions.

It can be used to criticize a person, a system, a plan, an institution, or even a thought process. It is flexible in who or what it can describe.
How It Differs from Simply Saying "Wrong"

Saying someone did something wrong is vague — they could have made a small error anywhere. Saying they did it bass-ackward is vivid and specific: it tells you the problem is one of orientation and order. The whole thing is pointed in the wrong direction. It's not a typo — it's a compass pointing south when it should point north.
Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture someone trying to use a hammer by holding the metal head and swinging the wooden handle at a nail. They're using a real hammer, they're putting in real effort, but the tool is completely reversed in their hand. That is "bass-ackward." The right ingredients, the right intentions, but the entire approach flipped around so that nothing works the way it should.
1553: A bassinet is a small, cosy bed made specifically for newborn babies and very young infants. Think of it as a baby's first sleeping space — smaller and more intimate than a full-sized crib, designed to hold a tiny baby safely while keeping them comfortable and close to their parents.

A bassinet typically has:

  • A soft, padded sleeping area — the interior is cushioned and lined with fabric to keep the baby comfortable and warm.
  • Rounded or oval shape — most bassinets are oval or oblong, which is gentler in appearance than the boxy shape of a crib.
  • A hood or canopy — many bassinets have a partial fabric canopy over one end, like a little shade or cover, to block light and give the baby a sense of shelter.
  • Legs or a stand — the sleeping basket sits on a frame, stand, or legs that raise it off the floor to a convenient height, usually level with an adult bed.
  • Mesh or fabric sides — the sides are often made of soft fabric, wicker, or breathable mesh (not solid wood bars like a crib).
  • Wheels — many modern bassinets have wheels or casters so parents can roll it from room to room easily.

Some bassinets also have a gentle rocking or swinging function to help soothe the baby to sleep.

A bassinet is used exclusively for newborns and very young babies, generally from birth up to around 3 to 6 months of age — or until the baby reaches the weight limit (usually around 9–15 kg / 20–33 lbs), or begins to push up on their hands or roll over on their own. Once a baby can do those things, a bassinet is no longer safe, and parents move the baby to a larger crib.
Why parents use a bassinet instead of going straight to a crib

The main reason is proximity and convenience. A bassinet is small and portable, so parents can place it right beside their own bed. This makes nighttime feeding and checking on the baby much easier — instead of walking to another room, the parent just reaches over. Newborns need to feed every 2–3 hours, so having the baby an arm's length away makes a significant difference, especially for breastfeeding mothers.

A bassinet also feels more womb-like and enclosed for a newborn. A full-sized crib can feel vast and cold to a tiny baby; a bassinet's snug interior can be more comforting.

Additionally, bassinets are lighter and more portable than cribs. Parents can move them to the living room during the day and back to the bedroom at night without difficulty.

• It is not a crib. A crib is a larger, sturdier, permanent bed — usually with solid sides made of wood or metal — designed for babies from a few months old up to toddler age. A bassinet is a temporary, transitional sleeping space used only in the first weeks or months of life.
  • It is not a Moses basket. A Moses basket is a similar concept — a small, portable basket for newborns — but it has no legs or stand of its own. It sits directly on the floor or a surface, and you carry it by handles like a shopping basket. A bassinet, by contrast, sits on its own stand or frame.
  • It is not a cradle. A cradle is a small baby bed that rocks from side to side on curved wooden rockers at the base, like a rocking chair lying on its side. It sits on the floor. A bassinet sits on a raised stand.
In everyday use (how the word appears in sentences)

• "We set up the bassinet right next to our bed so we could hear the baby at night."
  • "The baby outgrew her bassinet by the time she was four months old."
  • "He lined the bassinet with a soft blanket before bringing the newborn home from the hospital."
A bassinet is a small, soft, hooded baby bed raised on a stand, designed to hold a newborn safely and keep them within easy reach of their parents during the first few months of life.
1554: A bassoon is a large musical instrument that belongs to the woodwind family — the group of instruments in an orchestra that are traditionally made of wood and played by blowing air through them (like the flute, clarinet, and oboe). The bassoon is the lowest-pitched instrument among the standard woodwind instruments, meaning it plays deeper, heavier notes than its woodwind cousins.

At first glance, a bassoon looks like a tall, narrow bundle of tubes. It is roughly 1.2 metres (about 4 feet) tall when assembled, but if you were to unfold and straighten out all of its internal tubing, the full length would stretch to around 2.5 metres (over 8 feet). The tube doubles back on itself — going down and then back up — which is why the instrument is compact enough to hold despite being so long inside.

The body is usually made of maple wood and is dark brown in colour, with a large number of metal keys and pads running down its length. These keys cover the tone holes and are operated by the player's fingers. A thin curved metal tube, called the bocal (or crook), sticks out from the top of the instrument and connects to the mouthpiece.

The bassoon uses a double reed as its mouthpiece. A double reed is made of two thin, flat pieces of cane (a type of plant material) that are bound tightly together at one end, leaving a very narrow gap between them at the other end. The player places this reed between their lips and blows air through the gap. The two pieces of cane vibrate rapidly against each other, and this vibration travels down the long tube of the instrument, producing sound. The player changes the pitch (how high or low a note is) by pressing different combinations of keys.

This double-reed mechanism is the same one used by the oboe, which is the bassoon's higher-pitched relative. Because the bassoon's tube is so much longer, it produces much lower and deeper vibrations than the oboe.

The bassoon has a rich, dark, and slightly husky tone. Its sound is often described as warm and mellow in its lower notes, and slightly reedy or nasal in its higher range. It can sound solemn and dignified at slow speeds, but it can also sound remarkably comic, bumbling, or grumbling when played in a certain way — which is why composers sometimes use it to represent funny, grouchy, or clumsy characters in music. A famous example of this is in Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf, where the bassoon represents the grandfather — a slow, grumbling old man.

In an orchestra, the bassoon sits in the woodwind section and plays an important role in providing the bass foundation for that section — much like how a bass guitar holds down the low end in a band. It often plays alongside the cellos and double basses, adding depth and richness to the overall sound. It can also carry melodies on its own, especially in solo passages.

The bassoon typically covers a range of about three and a half octaves, from very deep notes to moderately high ones. It is used widely in:

  • Symphony orchestras (where there are usually two to four bassoons)
  • Wind ensembles and concert bands
  • Chamber music (small groups of instruments)
  • Solo performance (it has a rich repertoire of concertos and sonatas written for it)

Closely related to the bassoon is the contrabassoon (also called the double bassoon). It is an even larger instrument — if unfolded, its tubing would stretch to around 5.5 metres — and it plays an octave lower than the bassoon, producing some of the deepest notes found in a standard orchestra. It is used far less frequently and only appears when composers specifically call for it.
A person who plays the bassoon is called a bassoonist.

In older British English, the word "bassoon" was occasionally used informally as a mildly humorous insult for a pompous, foolish, or tiresome person — as in, "Don't be such an old bassoon." This usage is largely outdated and rarely encountered today, but it does appear in older literature.

A bassoon is a tall, wooden, double-reed woodwind instrument with a long folded tube and metal keys. It produces deep, rich, and characterful sound — capable of being both dignified and comic — and serves as the bass voice of the woodwind family in orchestras and ensembles around the world.
1555:
At its most literal, a bastard is a person born to parents who were not married to each other at the time of their birth. The word historically referred to a child considered "illegitimate" — meaning their birth fell outside the boundaries of legal marriage.

For most of human history, being a bastard was not just a label — it came with real consequences. Such a person could not legally inherit their father's title, land, or wealth. They had lower social standing than children born within marriage, and the word carried deep shame. Think of it as a kind of permanent social mark that followed a person their whole life, through no fault of their own.

This is the oldest and most literal sense of the word. Today, it still carries this meaning, but its weight has softened considerably — unmarried parenthood is no longer stigmatized the way it once was, so this specific meaning rarely comes up in everyday speech.
The Much More Common Modern Use: As an Insult

In everyday modern language, bastard is most often used as an insult directed at a person who behaves in a cruel, dishonest, unethical, or deeply unpleasant way.

When someone calls another person a bastard in this sense, they are not commenting on that person's birth parents at all. They are saying:

"This person is contemptible. They acted badly, unfairly, or wickedly."

Examples:

  • "He cheated on her for years and then blamed her for everything. What a bastard."
  • "That bastard stole money from his own employees."
  • "Don't trust him — he's a complete bastard."

The insult ranges in intensity depending on tone and context. At full force, it is a serious, harsh condemnation of someone's character or behavior. It says: this person has no decency.

This is considered a vulgar word — it is not appropriate in formal writing, professional settings, or polite company. However, in casual speech, it is used quite freely, especially in British English.

This is where the word becomes interesting, because bastard can be used in ways that carry zero hostility — and in fact, can express sympathy, affection, or even admiration.

1. The sympathetic "bastard"

When someone says "poor bastard," they are expressing genuine sympathy or pity. There is no insult here.

  • "He lost his job, then his wife left him, and now he's sick. Poor bastard."
  • "She had to work three jobs just to survive. Poor bastard."

The word here almost softens the speaker's tone — it signals that the speaker feels sorry for this person and sees them as a fellow human caught in unfortunate circumstances.

2. The envious "bastard"

When someone says "lucky bastard," they are expressing envy — sometimes playfully, sometimes genuinely.

  • "He won the lottery on his first ticket. Lucky bastard."
  • "She got promoted after just six months. Lucky bastard."

There is no real anger here. It is closer to: "I wish I were in that person's place."

3. The affectionate "bastard" (used between friends)

Among close friends, especially in British and Australian English, the word can be used affectionately — almost as a term of endearment, though a rough one.

  • "You old bastard, I haven't seen you in years! Come here!"
  • "He's a funny bastard, I'll give him that."

This only works when there is genuine warmth and closeness between the speakers. The same words from a stranger would land as a serious insult. Context and relationship are everything here.
For Something Difficult or Unpleasant (Not a Person)

The word can also be applied to things — not people — to describe something that is frustratingly hard, painful, or unpleasant to deal with.

  • "That exam was a real bastard." (It was extremely difficult.)
  • "The last mile of that hike was a total bastard." (It was brutal.)
  • "Getting that screw out was a bastard — it wouldn't budge."

Here the word functions as a way of expressing that something was unexpectedly, frustratingly tough. It has a kind of rueful humor to it.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Because this single word can mean so many different things, the meaning always depends on:

  • Tone of voice: Warm and laughing? Likely affectionate or sympathetic. Cold and contemptuous? It's an insult.
  • The word before it: Poor bastard = sympathy. Lucky bastard = envy. Old bastard = often affectionate. Complete bastard or total bastard = strong insult.
  • Who is speaking to whom: Close friends can use it casually. Between strangers or enemies, it is almost always hostile.
  • What it's describing: If it's a thing (a task, a problem), it means something is very hard or unpleasant.
The Register: When and Where Can You Use It?

• ❌ Formal writing, academic work, professional emails — avoid entirely.
  • ❌ Talking to people you don't know well — it may offend.
  • ✅ Casual conversation among friends — accepted, though still considered a mild expletive.
  • ✅ Reading literature, watching films, understanding dialogue — you'll encounter it frequently.

It is worth knowing that in British and Australian English, this word is used far more casually and frequently than in American English, where it tends to feel slightly more loaded.

Bastard originally meant a child born outside of marriage, and for centuries carried serious social and legal consequences. Today, it is rarely used in that literal sense. Instead, it functions primarily as an insult for a person who behaves cruelly or dishonestly, though it can also express sympathy (poor bastard), envy (lucky bastard), or even rough affection between friends. It can describe something extremely difficult or unpleasant as well. It is a vulgar word, best avoided in formal or polite contexts, but widely used in everyday informal speech — and its exact meaning in any given moment depends almost entirely on tone, context, and the relationship between the speakers.
1556:
When you bastardize something, you take something that was originally good, pure, genuine, or in its proper form — and you corrupt it, weaken it, or degrade it, usually by mixing it with something inferior, changing it carelessly, or stripping away what made it authentic. The result is a version that is worse, less genuine, or distorted compared to the original.

Think of it this way: if you have a beautiful, traditional recipe that has been passed down for generations, and someone comes along and replaces the key ingredients with cheap substitutes and calls it the same dish — they have bastardized that recipe.
The Two Senses of This Word

This word carries two distinct meanings, and you need to know both.

Sense 1 — The Common, Everyday Meaning (Used Most Often Today)

This is the sense you will encounter most frequently in modern speech and writing.

To bastardize something = to corrupt, debase, or degrade it from its original, authentic form — especially by mixing it poorly, simplifying it recklessly, or misrepresenting it.

The key feelings behind this word are:

  • Loss of quality
  • Loss of authenticity
  • A kind of disrespect toward the original

This word is especially used when talking about:

  • Language — when a language is mixed carelessly or degraded
  • Art, music, culture, food, or traditions — when something culturally significant is watered down or distorted
  • Ideas and concepts — when a complex idea is simplified so recklessly that it loses its real meaning

Examples:

  • "Hollywood has completely bastardized this novel. The film keeps the characters' names but throws away everything that made the book meaningful."

Here, the film has distorted the book so badly that it no longer represents what the original work truly was.

  • "Some critics argue that fast-food chains have bastardized Italian cuisine by replacing real ingredients with artificial substitutes just to cut costs."

The food still carries the Italian label, but its authenticity and quality have been destroyed.

  • "The politician bastardized the philosopher's ideas by quoting them out of context and twisting their meaning to serve his own agenda."

The original ideas were genuine and thoughtful; now they have been corrupted into something dishonest.

The emotional weight of this word:

"Bastardize" is not a neutral word. It carries a strong sense of disapproval and criticism. When someone says something has been bastardized, they are expressing that:

  1. The original was worth respecting.
  2. The person or process that changed it did so carelessly or dishonestly.
  3. The result is an inferior, inauthentic shadow of what it once was.

It is a word people use when they feel something valuable has been ruined.

Sense 2 — The Older, Formal/Legal Meaning (Less Common Today)

Historically and in formal/legal contexts, "bastardize" has carried a different and very specific meaning:

To bastardize someone = to officially declare or prove that a person is illegitimate — meaning they were born to parents who were not married to each other, and therefore have no legal right to inherit property, a title, or other privileges.

Example:

  • "The king's enemies sought to bastardize his son in court, hoping to prevent him from inheriting the throne."

In this sense, the word is almost purely a legal or historical term. You might encounter it when reading about monarchy, inheritance law, or historical novels. In everyday modern speech, this sense is rarely used.
The Connection Between the Two Senses

Both senses share the same underlying idea: something is being stripped of its rightful, legitimate status. In the legal sense, a person is declared not legitimate. In the modern sense, a thing — an idea, an art form, a tradition — is made illegitimate by being corrupted. The word travels from the personal to the conceptual, but the core feeling of degradation and loss of genuine status runs through both.

Several other words exist in the same neighborhood — words like corrupt, dilute, distort, dumb down, water down, debase, degrade, adulterate — but "bastardize" combines all of these ideas with an extra layer of meaning: the thing still pretends to be what it was. It still carries the original name or identity, but it has been hollowed out. It is a fake version wearing the costume of the real thing. That is what makes "bastardize" more specific and more powerful than simply saying something was "ruined."

This word is used in both spoken and written language, across formal essays, journalism, literary criticism, cultural commentary, and everyday conversation. It is not a slang word, but it is also not overly academic. It sits comfortably in the middle — usable in a serious editorial, a dinner-table argument about music, or a book review.

It is almost always used in a critical or negative tone. You will rarely, if ever, hear someone use "bastardize" approvingly.

What it meansTo corrupt, degrade, or debase something from its original genuine form — or (historically/formally) to declare a person legally illegitimate
ToneNegative and critical
Used most forCulture, art, language, ideas, traditions, concepts
Key feelingSomething authentic and valuable has been carelessly or dishonestly ruined, yet still claims the original's name
1557: The word baste has two completely different meanings depending on whether you're in a kitchen or working with fabric. It also has a third, older meaning.

To baste means to spoon, brush, or pour liquid over food — usually meat — while it is cooking, especially while it is roasting in an oven or grilling over heat.

The liquid used for basting can be:

  • The meat's own juices that collect at the bottom of the pan
  • Melted butter
  • A marinade, sauce, or broth
  • A mixture of any of these

Why do people baste?
When meat cooks in dry heat (like in an oven), its surface tends to dry out, become tough, and lose flavor. Basting solves this problem. Every time you spoon or brush liquid over the meat, that liquid:

  • Keeps the surface moist so it doesn't dry out or become leathery
  • Adds flavor with every coat of juice or sauce
  • Helps create a beautiful, glossy, golden-brown crust on the outside

How often do you baste?
Typically, you open the oven every 20–30 minutes and spoon the collected pan juices over the meat. Each time you do this, you are basting it.

Example:
"She basted the turkey every half hour so that it would come out juicy and golden."
"He basted the chicken with a mixture of honey, garlic, and butter."

The tool often used for this — a large bulb-shaped tube that sucks up liquid so you can squeeze it over meat — is called a basting syringe or baster. You can also simply use a spoon or a brush.

To baste means to sew pieces of fabric together using long, loose, temporary stitches.

These stitches are not meant to be permanent. They are deliberately made large and easy to remove. The purpose is to hold the fabric in place temporarily — like a pin, but with thread — so you can check the fit, alignment, or shape before you sew the final, permanent stitches.

Think of it as a "draft" stitch — just like you might write a rough draft of something before writing the final version.

Why is basting needed in sewing?

  • Pins can fall out or shift while you're working. Basting stitches hold everything more securely in place.
  • Before committing to permanent stitches on an expensive fabric, a tailor or seamstress baste-stitches first to make sure everything lines up correctly.
  • If something is wrong, you simply pull out the loose basting stitches (because they're long and easy to remove), adjust, and try again — without having damaged the fabric.

These temporary stitches are called basting stitches or sometimes just tacking stitches.

Example:
"She basted the hem before sewing it permanently, just to make sure it was even."
"He basted the two pieces of cloth together so they wouldn't slip under the sewing machine."

In older English and still occasionally in informal use, to baste can mean to hit or beat someone or something — to give someone a good thrashing.

Example:
"The villain threatened to baste him soundly if he didn't hand over the money."

This meaning is quite rare in modern everyday language, so you are far more likely to encounter it in older literature than in modern conversation. You do not need to use it yourself, but it's worth knowing so you're not confused if you come across it.
Quick Summary of All Three Meanings

In the kitchen: Baste = pour or brush liquid repeatedly over cooking food to keep it moist and flavorful.

In sewing: Baste = sew with long, loose, temporary stitches to hold fabric together before the final stitching.

In informal/old language: Baste = to beat or strike someone.

The cooking and sewing meanings are by far the most common and useful ones to know. Both involve a kind of "layering" or "going over" something repeatedly — liquid over meat, or thread over fabric — which is perhaps why the same word ended up covering both.
1558:
A bastion is a stronghold — a place, person, or thing that powerfully protects and preserves something, especially when that something is under threat or disappearing from the world around it.

Think of it this way: imagine a sandcastle being washed away by waves, but one solid, thick corner of it refuses to crumble. That corner is the bastion. It holds firm while everything else gives way.

The word has a literal meaning and a figurative meaning. Both are in active use.

1. The Literal Meaning (Physical/Military)

A bastion is a specific part of an old fort or castle — a thick, raised, outward-jutting structure built into a defensive wall, designed to give soldiers a position from which they could defend the surrounding walls from enemy attack. It was essentially the most heavily reinforced, strategically important section of a fortress. It didn't just protect itself — it helped protect everything else.

So in the physical world, a bastion is:

  • Part of a fortification (a walled defence structure)
  • Built to be especially strong and resistant
  • Positioned to defend and protect something larger

Example sentence: "The soldiers retreated to the bastion when the outer walls were breached."

2. The Figurative Meaning (Everyday Use — FAR More Common)

This is how most people use the word today. When we say something is a bastion, we mean it is a defender or guardian of something — a value, a tradition, a way of life, a belief, a right — especially when that thing is rare, threatened, or fading away in the wider world.

A bastion, in this sense, could be:

  • A place (a city, a country, an institution)
  • An organization (a university, a club, a company)
  • A group of people
  • Even a single person

The key feeling the word carries is: "This is one of the few places/things/people still standing strong for this cause or quality, while the rest of the world has moved away from it."

Example sentences:

  • "The old university was a bastion of free thought." (It fiercely protected the freedom to think and debate, even as other places didn't.)
  • "She was a bastion of integrity in a corrupt industry." (She was the rare, strong exception — someone who held firm to honesty when others around her didn't.)
  • "That small town remains a bastion of traditional culture." (The town has strongly preserved old customs that have vanished elsewhere.)

This is important to understand, because it gives the word its flavour.

"Bastion" is not a neutral word. It carries the feeling of:

  • Strength and resistance — it's not just "a place where X exists," it's "a place that actively stands firm for X."
  • Rarity — calling something a bastion quietly implies that it is one of the few remaining defenders of that thing. If the thing were common and unthreated, you wouldn't use this word.
  • Admiration OR criticism — depending on context, the word can be used approvingly or critically. For example, calling a company "a bastion of innovation" is a compliment. But calling a club "a bastion of outdated prejudice" is a criticism. The word itself is just saying "this place/thing strongly defends X" — whether X is good or bad depends on what's being defended.
The Underlying Logic: Why These Two Meanings Connect

The figurative meaning grew directly from the literal one. A military bastion was the part of a fortress that held its ground and protected what was inside. When people started using the word figuratively, they kept that exact idea: something that holds its ground and protects what it stands for, even under pressure. The image of a fortress wall that won't fall is baked right into the word.

What it isA stronghold; a powerful defender
What it defendsA value, belief, tradition, quality, or right
Key conditionUsually used when that thing is rare, threatened, or disappearing
ToneStrong, firm, resistant — can be admiring or critical
Most common useFigurative (people, places, institutions that defend something)
One Sentence to Remember It By
A bastion is the last strong wall standing — the person, place, or thing that firmly holds up and protects something important, even when the rest of the world no longer does.
1559:
To "not bat an eyelid" means to show absolutely no reaction — no surprise, no shock, no discomfort, and no emotion — even when something unusual, disturbing, or dramatic happens right in front of you.

A person who doesn't bat an eyelid stays completely calm, composed, and unmoved, as if nothing out of the ordinary is happening at all.

Notice the word "not" in that definition. This is important. The idiom is almost always used in the negative form. You will very rarely hear someone say "she batted an eyelid." Instead, you will almost always hear:

  • "She didn't bat an eyelid."
  • "He did it without batting an eyelid."
  • "They never batted an eyelid."
Why an Eyelid? Where Does This Come From?

This is a great question, because understanding the origin will lock the meaning in your memory permanently.

The word "bat" here is not the flying animal. It is a verb that means to flutter or to blink rapidly. It comes from an old French word batre, meaning to beat or to flap.

Now think about what happens to your eyes when you are suddenly surprised or shocked. Your eyelids flutter. You blink. Your eyes widen. These are tiny, automatic physical reactions that your body produces without you even thinking about it. You cannot easily control them. They are a natural signal to the world around you that you have been caught off guard.

So, "batting an eyelid" = the involuntary blinking or fluttering of the eyelid that happens when you are startled or emotionally affected.

Therefore, "not batting an eyelid" = your eyelids don't flutter at all = you show zero physical or emotional reaction. You are so calm, so cool, so in control — or so indifferent — that your body doesn't even flinch.

The idiom is used in everyday conversation and writing. Here are examples across different situations to show you its full range:

Example 1 — Shocking news:
"I told him his flight had been cancelled and he would miss the wedding, but he didn't bat an eyelid. He just calmly booked another one."
Here, the person showed no stress or frustration whatsoever.

Example 2 — An outrageous price:
"The restaurant charged her £500 for dinner, and she paid without batting an eyelid."
Here, she didn't react to the price at all — suggesting it was no big deal to her.

Example 3 — A dangerous or frightening situation:
"The soldier walked through the burning building without batting an eyelid."
Here, it suggests remarkable bravery and calmness under extreme pressure.

Example 4 — Something morally wrong:
"He lied to his entire team and didn't bat an eyelid."
Here, the idiom takes on a darker, more negative tone — he felt no guilt or discomfort about doing something wrong.

Example 5 — An unusual or bizarre event:
"A man walked into the office wearing a full clown costume, and the receptionist didn't bat an eyelid — she'd seen stranger things."
Here, she was so used to unusual events that this one didn't surprise her at all.

This idiom can carry two very different feelings depending on the context, and you must read the situation carefully.

1. Positive or admirable meaning:
Sometimes, not batting an eyelid is a sign of strength, courage, or professionalism. A surgeon who stays calm during a crisis, a pilot who handles an emergency without panicking, a negotiator who doesn't flinch when the other side makes an outrageous demand — these are all positive examples. It means the person has impressive self-control.

2. Negative or cold meaning:
Other times, not batting an eyelid is a sign of callousness, indifference, or cruelty. If someone hears that a friend is suffering and doesn't bat an eyelid, it means they simply don't care. This use of the idiom suggests the person should have reacted but chose not to — or simply felt nothing at all.

The words around the idiom will always tell you which meaning applies.

"Bat an eyelid" is the version most commonly used in British English.

In American English, people more often say "bat an eye" or sometimes "bat an eyelash". All three mean exactly the same thing. If you learn one, you know all three.

  • British: "She didn't bat an eyelid."
  • American: "She didn't bat an eye."
Register — When Should You Use It?

This idiom is informal to neutral. It fits naturally in:

  • Everyday conversation with friends or colleagues
  • Novels, short stories, and journalism
  • Informal essays or blog posts

It would sound slightly out of place in a very formal academic paper or a legal document, but in almost every other setting, it is perfectly appropriate.

Knowing related expressions helps you understand the idiom even more deeply.

  • "Not turn a hair" — very similar; means to remain totally calm and undisturbed.
  • "Not flinch" — to not make any sudden movement of fear or pain; very close in meaning.
  • "Keep a stiff upper lip" — to suppress emotion and stay composed, especially under hardship.
  • "Cool as a cucumber" — completely relaxed and unrattled in a difficult situation.
  • "Unflappable" — an adjective for a person who cannot be made nervous or upset.

All of these share the idea of staying calm and showing no reaction, but "not bat an eyelid" is particularly vivid because it focuses on that tiny, telling flicker of the eye that gives our feelings away — and says: not even that happened.

Core meaningTo show no reaction, surprise, or emotion whatsoever
Almost always used asNegative — "didn't bat an eyelid," "without batting an eyelid"
Origin"Bat" = to flutter; eyelids naturally flutter when we're startled
Can meanBravery/composure OR coldness/indifference, depending on context
British version"Bat an eyelid"
American version"Bat an eye" / "bat an eyelash"

The beauty of this idiom is how physical and human it is. It roots itself in something every single person on earth does involuntarily — blinking in surprise — and then describes someone who doesn't even do that. That image alone should make it impossible to forget.
